name: Q: 'Which engine for structured output / agentic / multi-turn workloads?' - A: SGLang and vLLM, with the reason stated as prefix reuse, and llama.cpp kept for the local-model reference path
symptom: For prefix-heavy and structured work the corpus names vLLM's prefix caching as the specific asset: 'Prefix caching is amazing for best-of-n style generative tasks.' For large-context single-box work on current NVIDIA hardware the advice is to leave a simple local stack for a served engine, 126 upvotes: 'You need to be using sglang or vLLM with that 6000. It's significantly faster due to MTP support and significantly better with large context.' Multi-turn and agentic traffic is where the two engines are said to differ, with multinode setup - not throughput - as the deciding factor for SGLang. Against that, llama.cpp holds the local-model and consumer slots on the strength of quant coverage and hardware breadth, and one commenter calls llama.cpp 'by far the best' for a single user on a single card while conceding 'If more than four concurrent users with high access rate then vLLM starts to make more sense.'
root_cause: Prefix reuse is the mechanism the community actually names, and it is the property that structured and multi-turn traffic monetises: a long system prompt, tool schemas and prior turns are identical across requests, so a prefix cache converts them from per-request prefill into a cache hit. That is why the recommendation is tied to workload shape rather than to model size. The counterweight is that this advantage requires the engine to be holding a KV cache across requests, which is precisely what the single-process local stacks are not built for.
workaround: For repeated system prompts, tool schemas, best-of-n sampling, or long multi-turn sessions, choose an engine with prefix caching and measure cache hit rate on your own traffic. Keep llama.cpp as the reference path for local models and unusual quant formats; the corpus recommends running both rather than committing.
notes: Recorded honestly as a soft consensus. The corpus contains no practitioner claim that SGLang's RadixAttention specifically is why to prefer it for prefix workloads - that argument comes from vendor-adjacent sources, and the practitioner threads here justify the choice by prefix caching generically, multinode setup simplicity, and MTP support. Also note the engine-agnostic variant of the same advice from a startup launch thread: 'It's resending the same system prompt plus tool schemas every turn', which a commenter identifies as the real cost, above decode speed.
